newsitem.title: UK: Profile of Labour's new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Profile of Labour's new cabinet.

text.p: Tony Blair on Saturday announced his his first cabinet as Labour Prime Minister.
Following is a list of short profiles of the new cabinet:
PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR (Born 6/5/53)

Tony Blair, whose boyish looks belie a steely determination to win power, wasted no time when he became Labour leader in July 1994 in dumping the ideological baggage that had cost the party four general elections

He shocked Labour's annual conference by announcing plans to rewrite the party's Marxist constitution and openly wooed middle-class voters by embracing free-market economics and keeping trade unions at arm's length.

By anchoring Labour in the mainstream of British politics, Blair carved out a huge poll lead but his tight grip on the party also angered left-wing activists resentful of their waning influence. His election victory was Labour's biggest ever.
DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER JOHN PRESCOTT (Born 31/05/38)

Blunt and forthright by nature, John Prescott has had to bite his tongue since becoming the Labour party's deputy leader in 1994. But his forceful presence behind the scenes, both physically and verbally, has been crucial to party unity.
A ship's steward who regularly clashed with officers, he became a union leader and driving force behind a 1966 seamen's strike before going to university to study economics.
He failed to win the top job after John Smith died, settling instead for deputy, where his traditional left-wing credentials have balanced the modernising zeal of Labour leader Tony Blair.
Despite his mangled syntax, Prescott is a rousing orator. But under a bluff exterior, friends say the jazz-loving railway worker's son is still afraid of being put down.
CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER GORDON BROWN (Born 20/2/51)

Brown, whose decision not to contest the Labour Party leadership contest in 1994 virtually handed victory to Tony Blair, has been rewarded with the leading role in the most sensitive area for Labour's new government.
He has cleverly identified areas where the Conservatives are vulnerable, such as directors' pay and perks, and has forged a new image of a party eager to cut taxes on ordinary Britons.
It was his decision to pledge to stick to the government's spending targets and to rule out any increase in income tax which is seen as one of the key reasons for Labour's victory.
FOREIGN SECRETARY ROBIN COOK (Born 28/2/46)

Probably the sharpest mind on the Labour front bench and the best debater by far, Robin Cook reluctantly surrendered the trade and industry portfolio in 1994 at new leader Tony Blair's request to give a sharper edge to the party's policy on Europe.

A brilliant, incisive debater, Cook has a healthy scepticism toward Europe. On a single currency, for instance, he says the economic convergence criteria for membership must be complemented by benchmarks for employment and competitiveness.

Cook, who finds time to be a horseracing tipster for a Scottish newspaper, wryly acknowledges that his gnome-like looks -- a diminutive frame, furrowed brow and pointed red beard -- rule him out as a future Labour leader in the television age.
HOME SECRETARY JACK STRAW (Born 3/8/46)

No one better typifies the rightward shift of the Labour Party under Tony Blair than Straw, a former student leader who showed a distinct reluctance to criticise the law-and-order policies pushed forward by the Conservatives.

Straw, who held a variety of party spokesmanships before being given home affairs in 1994, refused even to attack his opponent Michael Howard over plans to give the police powers to bug suspects homes until goaded into it by other opposition politicians.
His reluctance may owe something to the fact that he has been consistently worsted by Howard when the two have clashed in major parliamentary debates.
Straw, a lawyer who came into parliament at the 1979 election when the Conservatives win power, is a former deputy leader of the Inner London Education Authority.
TRADE AND INDUSTRY SECRETARY MARGARET BECKETT (Born 15/01/43)

Beckett briefly became the Party's first woman leader when she stepped in as caretaker after John Smith's death in 1994. But she ran third behind Tony Blair and John Prescott in the election which followed.

She has shown a fierce loyalty to Labour and has few enemies, but is sometimes regarded as showing a lack of principle because of her willingness to move with the party's political tide. She is still considered to be on the left of much of Blair's cabinet.
SOCIAL SECURITY SECRETARY HARRIET HARMAN (Born 30/7/50)
Attractive and articulate, Harman projects perfectly the moderate middle-class image of Labour under Tony Blair.

But she infuriated old-Labour traditionalists in January 1996 for sending her son to a selective grammar school -- in defiance of party policy -- and kept her job only thanks to unflinching support from Blair, who had done the same thing.
Blair also made a point of keeping her on Labour's front bench when she was voted off the shadow cabinet in 1994 and gave her a big promotion to the health portfolio the following year.
Married to a leading trade unionist, Harman was a prominent civil liberties' activist before entering parliament in 1982.
HERITAGE SECRETARY CHRIS SMITH (Born 24/7/51)
A former president of Cambridge Union and Kennedy scholar at Harvard, Smith has been asked by Labour leader Tony Blair "to think the unthinkable" on welfare reform.

Smith has a doctorate in early 19th-century English poetry and is a governor of a theatre and orchestra in his London constituency of Islington, which made him an obvious choice for his previous job as shadow national heritage spokesman.
In that capacity he played a cruciaal role developing Blair's eye-catching proposal for BT to wire up all schools, hospitals and libraries to the information superhighway.
Smith, from the soft left wing of the party, is the only MP to have climbed all 277 hills exceeding 3,000ft in Scotland - and the only one to have declared his homosexuality openly.
He was moved by Blair from the health portfolio he held before the election back to the cabinet's heritage because of some friction over health policy with the Labour leadership.
EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT SECRETARY DAVID BLUNKETT (Born 06/06/47)

David Blunkett's start in life was far from easy. Born blind, he was written off by his first school, which suggested he find a job as a piano tuner or lathe operator. His father died when he was just 12, victim of a horrific work accident.
But a determination to overcome his disability took him through university, where he studied politics. From his childhood, he inherited a deep sense of injustice.

His path to parliament was smooth after a widely praised stint as head of the council in the northern city of Sheffield. A member of parliament since 1987, he has turned education into a key electoral battleground. Straddling the left-right divide, he has become a key member of Labour leader Tony Blair's team.
HEALTH SECRETARY FRANK DOBSON (Born 15/3/40)

A bouncy, pugnacious Yorkshire terrier, Dobson loves nothing so much as picking up an issue, such as leakages at privatised water companies, and pursuing it until it becomes a major embarassment to the government.
This tenacity won him promotion from transport spokesman and despite his reputation as a member of the soft Left, he was rewarded with Health, one of the big spending departments.
CHANCELLOR OF THE DUCHY OF LANCASTER (RESPONSIBLE FOR THE CIVIL SERVICE) DAVID CLARK (Born 19/10/39)

Clark, who made his name as a campaigner for the environment, was a defence spokesman since 1992 despite his membership of parliamentary Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament in the mid-1980s. While hardworking and worthy, the former lecturer, a Scot with a north of England seat has failed to make a major impact in opposition.
AGRICULTURE SECRETARY JACK CUNNINGHAM (Born 4/8/39)

Cunningham is one of the few to have seen a Labour government from the inside, having been parliamentary private secretary to Foreign Secretary James Callaghan from 1974 to 1976 and a junior energy minister for the next three years.
But his political fortunes suffered a setback in recent years and he was demoted from the foreign affairs portfolio. He is not a natural parliamentary performer.

He has worked hard to carve out a distinctive policy on the national lottery, calling for a non-profit making body to take over from the present Camelot consortium when its seven-year franchise runs out.
TRANSPORT SECRETARY SPOKESMAN GAVIN STRANG (Born 10/7/43)
Strang, a junior agriculture minister in the last Labour government, hoed the same row in opposition since 1992.
WELSH SECRETARY RON DAVIES (Born 6/8/46)

A typical product of the South Wales Labour Party, Davies was elected to parliament in 1983 after 14 years as a local councillor and shortly afterwards took on a junior job as a spokesman on agriculture.
He became shadow Welsh Secretary in 1992, and has sought to keep a balance between keen devolutionists and party members who have little enthusiasm for a Welsh Assembly.
LEADER OF THE HOUSE ANN TAYLOR (Born 2/7/47)

A strong-chinned, straight-talking blonde, Taylor has peformed more strongly in her current job than in her previous post as education spokeswoman, where her policy proposals were promptly rejected by Blair when he became leader.
She started in parliament as a leftish Tribune Group member but is now anchored firmly in New Labour's moderate mainstream.
CHIEF SECRETARY TO THE TREASURY ALISTAIR DARLING (Born 28/11/53)
Another able Scottish lawyer, Darling won promotion to the job of Gordon Brown's deputy after his impressive handling of the tricky financial services and City regulation portfolio.

More at ease with detailed arguments than snappy soundbites, the former Scottish regional councillor entered parliament in 1987 and was quickly marked down as one of the brightest of Labour's new intake.
NORTHERN IRELAND SECRETARY MARJORIE MOWLAM (Born 18/9/49)
A bubbly, extrovert politician, "Mo" Mowlem has scrupulously upheld Labour's policy of cooperation with the government over Northern Ireland.
She caused a stir in her previous post as national heritage spokesman by proposing that Buckingham Palace be turned into a "people's palace".
DEFENCE SECRETARY GEORGE ROBERTSON (Born 12/4/46)

Dithering last summer by Labour's Scottish leadership over the mechanics of a referendum to endorse plans for a parliament in Edinburgh reflected badly on Robertson, a canny, articulate Scot who used to hold Labour's European affairs portfolio.

A former trade unionist, his profile increased after the massacre of 16 children and their teacher at Dunblane primary school near his home. He has always been opposed to unilateral nuclear disarmament.
LEADER OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS LORD RICHARD OF AMMANFORD (Born 30/5/32)

Was Labour's leader in the House of Lords for five years while in opposition. Lord Richard, a barrister, was Britain's Permanent Representative at the United Nations from 1974 to 1979. Previously, he was Labour MP for Baron's Court in west London from 1964 to 1974.
SCOTTISH SECRETARY DONALD DEWAR (Born 21/8/37)
A former chief whip considered to have performed well. Bright, industrious and able, he was a close friend of Labour leader John Smith, who died in 1994.
He has a legal mind and is tipped to be a key figure in guiding Blair's devolution legislation through parliament.
LORD CHANCELLOR LORD IRVINE (Born 23/6/40)
Blair and his wife Cherie met while they were learning the law under Irvine and he has remained a close confidant of the Labour leader since those days.
INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT SECRETARY CLARE SHORT (Born 15/2/46)
Plain speaking advocate of women's rights who got herself into trouble during the election campaign with loose talk on the legalisation of cannabis. She was openly critical of Labour's spin doctors.
She made no secret of her displeasure when Blair removed her from the high-profile job as shadow transport secretary to the relative backwater of overseas development.
